text: Resistors, diodes and jumper wires arrive on tape, lined up and ready. So why does someone still cut and bend every one of them by hand?
On the left, manual cut and form. On the right, the Southern Machinery S A F 1001 axial tape feeder.
By hand, the operator cuts each part off the tape, bends both leads in a jig, and hands it to the machine. The insertion head waits, and the pin spacing changes from one part to the next.

The S A F 1001 indexes the tape with a hardened steel ratchet driven by an air cylinder, while an anti-reversal pawl holds every pitch. A fibre sensor confirms the part is in the station. Then one cylinder stroke cuts the leads and forms them into a U, the part is presented to the head, and the waste tape drops out of the front.
The result: one formed part every zero point eight seconds, at plus or minus zero point three millimetres, with air pressure speed regulation.

High carbon steel blades shear the leads, and the male die bends them over the female die into a clean U. To change pin spacing, you move the forming die blocks, and every part after that comes out the same.

It runs standard bandoleer tape, twenty-six or fifty-two millimetres wide, with thirty-five, sixty-four and ninety-two millimetre versions on request. Resistors, diodes, inductors, capacitors and jumper wires, with bodies from three by three to six by twenty millimetres and leads up to one millimetre.

At seven hundred and thirty millimetres long and eight kilograms, it runs on twenty-four volts and factory air. One eight-core aviation plug carries the request, part present, cut complete and tape empty signals, or it runs on its own.
Tested for one thousand consecutive feeds without a misfeed, and forty-eight hours of continuous operation without failure. No bench, no hand-bent leads, and a head that keeps inserting.
